**Sarah Elizabeth Huckabee Sanders** (born August 13, 1982)[[1]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-SHSbirthdate-1) is an American politician serving since 2023 as the 47th [governor of Arkansas](Governor_of_Arkansas "Governor of Arkansas").

Sanders is the daughter of [Mike Huckabee](Mike_Huckabee "Mike Huckabee"), who served from 1996 to 2007 as Arkansas's 44th governor.[[2]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-2) A member of the [Republican Party](Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)"), she was the 31st [White House press secretary](White_House_press_secretary "White House press secretary"), serving under President [Donald Trump](Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") from 2017 to 2019. Sanders was the third woman to be White House press secretary.[[3]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:6-3) She also served as a senior advisor on [Trump's 2016 presidential campaign](Donald_Trump_2016_presidential_campaign "Donald Trump 2016 presidential campaign"). Sanders became the [Republican](Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nominee in the [2022 Arkansas gubernatorial election](2022_Arkansas_gubernatorial_election "2022 Arkansas gubernatorial election") and won, defeating Democratic nominee [Chris Jones](Christopher_M._Jones_(politician) "Christopher M. Jones (politician)").

As press secretary, Sanders was the spokesperson for the Trump administration's policy decisions, and had a confrontational relationship with the [White House press corps](White_House_press_corps "White House press corps").[[4]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-4)[[5]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-5)[[6]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-6)[[7]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-7) When interviewed by investigators as part of the [Mueller probe](Mueller_special_counsel_investigation "Mueller special counsel investigation"), she admitted making false statements in her role.[[8]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:4-8)[[9]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:3-9)[[10]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:5-10) Sanders hosted fewer press conferences than any of the 13 previous White House press secretaries.[[11]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-11)

In June 2019, Trump tweeted that Sanders would be leaving her role as press secretary.[[12]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-ABC_News-12)[[13]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-nytimes.com-13) On January 25, 2021, she announced her candidacy for governor of Arkansas; Trump endorsed her. She secured the Republican nomination in May 2022; her general election opponents were the [Democratic](Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") nominee, Chris Jones, and the [Libertarian](Libertarian_Party_(United_States) "Libertarian Party (United States)") nominee, Ricky Dale Harrington. She is the first woman to hold the office, the first woman to be governor of a state of which her father was also governor,[[14]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-auto-14)[[15]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-auto1-15) and the youngest current governor.[[16]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-16)

Sanders has been recognized in *[Fortune](Fortune_(magazine) "Fortune (magazine)")* and *[Time](Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* magazine's "40 under 40". She is the author of *[The New York Times](The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* bestseller *Speaking for Myself*, is a former [Fox News Channel](Fox_News_Channel "Fox News Channel") contributor, and served on the [Fulbright](Fulbright_Program "Fulbright Program") board.[[3]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:6-3)

## Early life and education

Sarah Elizabeth Huckabee was born on August 13, 1982, in [Hope, Arkansas](Hope%2C_Arkansas "Hope, Arkansas").[[1]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-SHSbirthdate-1) She is the youngest child and only daughter of [Mike Huckabee](Mike_Huckabee "Mike Huckabee") and [Janet Huckabee](Janet_Huckabee "Janet Huckabee") (*née* McCain), both politicians.[[17]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-Star-17)[[18]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-Heavy-18) She has two brothers, John Mark Huckabee and David Huckabee.[[18]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-Heavy-18) After graduating from [Little Rock Central High School](Little_Rock_Central_High_School "Little Rock Central High School") in [Little Rock, Arkansas](Little_Rock%2C_Arkansas "Little Rock, Arkansas"),[[19]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-AT2-19) Huckabee attended [Ouachita Baptist University](Ouachita_Baptist_University "Ouachita Baptist University") (her father's alma mater) in [Arkadelphia, Arkansas](Arkadelphia%2C_Arkansas "Arkadelphia, Arkansas"). She was elected [student body president](Student-body_president "Student-body president") of the university and was active in Republican organizations. In 2004, she graduated from the university with a Bachelor of Arts degree, majoring in [political science](Political_science "Political science") and minoring in [mass communications](Mass_communication "Mass communication").[[20]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-20)[[21]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-21)[[22]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-ouachitadegree-22)

## Career

### Early political career

Sanders was involved in her father's first campaign for the [United States Senate](United_States_Senate "United States Senate") in 1992. Describing the unsuccessful bid in an interview for *[The Hill](The_Hill_(newspaper) "The Hill (newspaper)")*, she said: "He didn't really have much of a staff, so our family has been very engaged and very supportive of my dad. I was stuffing envelopes, I was knocking on doors, I was putting up yard signs."[[18]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-Heavy-18) Her father said of her childhood, "I always say that when most kids are seven or eight years old out jumping rope, she was sitting at the kitchen table listening to political commentators analyze poll results." Huckabee said that he and his wife spoiled Sarah at times. He called her "doggone tough" and "fearless" due to having grown up with two brothers.[[23]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:1-23)

Sanders was a field coordinator for her father's [2002 reelection campaign](Arkansas_gubernatorial_election%2C_2002 "Arkansas gubernatorial election, 2002") for [governor of Arkansas](Governor_of_Arkansas "Governor of Arkansas"). Sanders is a founding partner of Second Street Strategies in Little Rock, a general consulting services provider[[26]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-2ndStStratArchive-26) for Republican campaigns.[[27]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-27) She worked on national political campaigns and campaigns for federal office in Arkansas. Sanders was also vice president of [Tsamoutales Strategies](Frank_Tsamoutales "Frank Tsamoutales").[[25]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-archive.org-25) She was national political director for her father's [2008 presidential campaign](Mike_Huckabee_presidential_campaign%2C_2008 "Mike Huckabee presidential campaign, 2008").[[3]](Sarah_Huckabee_Sanders#cite_note-:6-3) She was also a senior adviser to [Tim Pawlenty](Tim_Pawlenty "Tim Pawlenty") in his 2012 presidential run. **Andrew Graham Beshear** (born November 29, 1977) is an American attorney and politician who has served as the 63rd [governor of Kentucky](Governor_of_Kentucky "Governor of Kentucky") since 2019. From 2016 to 2019, he served as the 50th [attorney general of Kentucky](Attorney_General_of_Kentucky "Attorney General of Kentucky"). A member of the [Democratic Party](Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), he is the son of [Steve Beshear](Steve_Beshear "Steve Beshear"), the 61st governor of Kentucky.

Beshear was elected attorney general in [November 2015](2015_Kentucky_elections#Attorney_General "2015 Kentucky elections") and took office in January 2016. As attorney general, he sued Governor [Matt Bevin](Matt_Bevin "Matt Bevin") several times over issues such as pensions. He then defeated Bevin by just over 5,000 votes in the [2019 gubernatorial election](2019_Kentucky_gubernatorial_election "2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election"). As of 2023, Beshear and Lieutenant Governor [Jacqueline Coleman](Jacqueline_Coleman "Jacqueline Coleman") are Kentucky's only Democratic statewide elected officials.

## Early life and education

Beshear was born in Louisville, the son of Steve and [Jane Beshear](Jane_Beshear "Jane Beshear").[[1]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-1) He graduated from [Henry Clay High School](Henry_Clay_High_School "Henry Clay High School") in [Lexington, Kentucky](Lexington%2C_Kentucky "Lexington, Kentucky").[[2]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-2) His father, a lawyer and politician, was the governor of Kentucky from 2007 to 2015.[[3]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-3)

Beshear attended [Vanderbilt University](Vanderbilt_University "Vanderbilt University") in <Tennessee>, where he was a member of the [Sigma Chi Fraternity](Sigma_Chi "Sigma Chi") and graduated in 2000 with a bachelor's degree in anthropology.[[4]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-4)[[5]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-5) He then attended the [University of Virginia School of Law](University_of_Virginia_School_of_Law "University of Virginia School of Law"), where he received a Juris Doctor in 2003.[[6]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-6)

## Legal career

In 2005, Beshear was hired by the law firm [Stites & Harbison](Stites_%26_Harbison "Stites & Harbison"), at which his father was a partner.[[7]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-7)[[8]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-profile-8)[[9]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-9) He represented the developers of the Bluegrass Pipeline, which would have transported [natural gas liquid](Natural_gas_liquid "Natural gas liquid") through Kentucky. The project was controversial; critics voiced environmental concerns and objections to the use of [eminent domain](Eminent_domain "Eminent domain") for the pipeline. His father's office maintained that there was no conflict of interest with the son's representation.[[10]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-10)[[11]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-11)[[12]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-12)[[13]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-13) Beshear also represented the Indian company UFLEX, which sought $20 million in tax breaks from his father's administration, drawing criticism from ethics watchdogs over a potential conflict of interest.[[14]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-14)

## Kentucky Attorney General

### Elections

#### 2015

Main article: [2015 Kentucky elections § Attorney General](2015_Kentucky_elections#Attorney_General "2015 Kentucky elections")

Beshear defeated [Republican](Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") [Whitney Westerfield](Whitney_Westerfield "Whitney Westerfield") with 50.1% of the vote to Westerfield's 49.9%.[[17]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-17)[[18]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-18) The margin was approximately 2,000 votes.[[19]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-19)

#### Tenure

Beshear sued Governor [Matt Bevin](Matt_Bevin "Matt Bevin") several times over what he argued was Bevin's abuse of executive powers during Beshear's tenure as attorney general and while he was campaigning against Bevin for governor.[[20]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-auto15-20) Beshear won some cases and lost others.[[20]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-auto15-20) In April 2016, he sued Bevin over his mid-cycle budget cuts to the state university system.[[21]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-21) The [Kentucky Supreme Court](Kentucky_Supreme_Court "Kentucky Supreme Court") issued a 5–2 ruling agreeing with Beshear that Bevin did not have the authority to make mid-cycle budget cuts without the [Kentucky General Assembly](Kentucky_General_Assembly "Kentucky General Assembly")'s approval.[[22]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-22) Also in 2016, the Kentucky Supreme Court unanimously sided with Bevin when Beshear sued him on the grounds that Bevin lacked the authority to overhaul the [University of Louisville's](University_of_Louisville "University of Louisville") board of trustees.[[23]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-23) In 2017, the Kentucky Supreme Court threw out a lawsuit Beshear brought against Bevin, holding that Bevin had the power to temporarily reshape boards while the legislature is out of session; Bevin called Beshear's lawsuit a "shameful waste of taxpayer resources".[[24]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-24) In April 2018, Beshear successfully sued Bevin for signing [Senate Bill 151](2018_Kentucky_Senate_Bill_151 "2018 Kentucky Senate Bill 151"), a controversial plan to reform teacher pensions, with the Kentucky Supreme Court ruling the bill unconstitutional.[[25]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-25)[[26]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-:0-26)[[27]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-27) Bevin said Beshear "never sues on behalf of the people of Kentucky. He does it on behalf of his own political career".[[28]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-28)

Throughout October 2019, Beshear filed nine lawsuits against pharmaceutical companies for their alleged involvement in fueling Kentucky's [opioid epidemic](Opioid_epidemic "Opioid epidemic").[[29]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-29)[[30]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-30)

Beshear forwent a run for a second term as attorney general to run for governor against Bevin. He resigned from the attorney general's office on December 10, 2019, to be sworn in as governor. He was succeeded as attorney general by [Daniel Cameron](Daniel_Cameron_(American_politician) "Daniel Cameron (American politician)") on December 17.[[31]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-31)

## Governor of Kentucky

#### 2019

Main article: [2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election](2019_Kentucky_gubernatorial_election "2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election")

Beshear faced incumbent Governor [Matt Bevin](Matt_Bevin "Matt Bevin"), the nation's least popular governor, in the November 5 general election.[[37]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-37)[[38]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-38)[[39]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-39) He defeated Bevin with 49.20% of the vote to Bevin's 48.83%.[[40]](Andy_Beshear#cite_note-:2-40) It was the closest Kentucky gubernatorial election ever by percentage, and the closest race of the [2019 gubernatorial election cycle](2019_Un

**Joshua David Shapiro** (born June 20, 1973)[[1]](Josh_Shapiro#cite_note-1) is an American politician and attorney who has served as the 48th [governor of Pennsylvania](Governor_of_Pennsylvania "Governor of Pennsylvania") since 2023.
